input: When a science becomes successful, it eventually stops using rough laws based on probable sequences and uses a completely different kind of law instead. Daily life and early science depend on these probable patterns. But they get set aside as field grows more advanced. The law of gravitation is an example of what happens in any advanced science. When bodies pull on each other through gravity, nothing is really a cause. And nothing is really an effect. There is only a formula. Certain differential equations apply at every moment to every particle in the system. If you know the positions and speeds at one moment, or the positions at two moments, you can in theory work out the positions at any other moment, before or after. In other words, the positions at any time are a function of that time and the positions at two given times. This is true for all of physics, not just gravity. But in a system like this, nothing deserves to be called a "cause" or an "effect." The old law of causality stays in philosophy books mostly because most philosophers are not familiar with the idea of a function, so they look for a statement that is too simple. There is no question of the same cause happeinng again to make the same effect. The steadiness of scientific law is based not on causes and effects beign the same but on relations being the same.
